questions.question: Explain any three maternal factors that affect the prenatal development.
questions.solution_html:
• Explain any three maternal factors that affect the prenatal development.  /
  • [CO2]
  • Maternal exercise, nutrition, Emotional well-being, mother’s age is major maternal factors
  • that affect prenatal development.
  • Exercise: Moderate exercise (walking, swimming, biking, and aerobics) is beneficial — it
  • increases birth weight and reduces risks of complications such as: Pregnancy-induced
  • diabetes, High blood pressure. Excessive vigorous exercise can lower birth weight.
  • Nutrition: Healthy diet with weight gain supports mother and baby’s health. Malnutrition
  • in First trimester leads to miscarriages, physical defects. Later malnutrition results in low
  • birth weight, small head size. The malnutrition mother can result in brain damage, Organ
  • defects, Low Immunity, Low Intelligence, Behavioural Problem
  • Maternal Stress: Severe maternal stress especially in 1st–2nd trimester may cause risk of
  • miscarriage, prematurity, low birth weight, illness, and sleep and behaviour problems.
  • Stress hormones increase fetal heart rate, BP, glucose, long-term risk of heart disease &
  • diabetes.
  • Maternal Age: Delayed childbearing increase the risk miscarriage, chromosomal defects.
  • Risks increase sharply after 40
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Analyse the role of prescription and non-prescription drugs as teratogens.
questions.solution_html:
• Analyse the role of prescription and non-prescription drugs as teratogens.
  • / [CO2]
  • Teratogens are environmental agents that can cause prenatal damage or interfere with normal
  • development. Some prescription drugs taken during pregnancy can cross the placenta and
  • reach the developing organism. The effects depend on the type and dosage of the drug,
  • duration of exposure and timing of exposure during prenatal development.
  • Drug exposure can result in physical abnormalities, impaired growth, damage to
  • developing organs, brain or nervous-system abnormalities and later behavioural or
  • cognitive problems. Eg : thalidomide, a prescription drug that, when taken during early
  • pregnancy, was associated with severe limb abnormalities and other congenital defects in
  • developing babies.
  • Some non-prescription or over-the-counter drugs may also produce harmful effects when
  • used without appropriate medical guidance. Eg : aspirin (salicylates), particularly in high
  • doses or later pregnancy, may increase the risk of bleeding and other pregnancy-related
  • complications. Therefore, non-prescription drugs should not automatically be considered
  • harmless during pregnancy.

questions.question: Explain how the exosystem differs from the macrosystem in the ecological system theory
questions.solution_html:
• Explain how the exosystem differs from the macrosystem in the ecological system
  • theory.  / [CO3]
  • The exosystem consists of links between a social setting in which the individual does not
  • have an active role and the individual’s immediate context. For example child’s experience at
  • home may be influenced by a mother’s experiences at work
  • The macrosystem involves the culture in which individuals live. Culture refers to the
  • behavior patterns, beliefs, and all other products of a group of people that are passed on from
  • generation to generation.

questions.question: Describe the phallic stage of psychosexual theory in detail.
questions.solution_html:
• Describe the phallic stage of psychosexual theory in detail. / [CO3]
  • The phallic stage is the third stage of Freud's psychosexual theory, occurring
  • approximately between 3 and 6 years of age. During this stage, the genital region becomes
  • the primary focus of pleasure.
  • According to Freud, children develop unconscious feelings toward the parent of the opposite
  • sex. In boys, this is described as the Oedipus complex, involving affection toward the
  • mother and rivalry with the father. In girls, Freud proposed the Electra complex, involving
  • affection toward the father and rivalry with the mother. Freud also proposed penis envy in
  • girls, referring to the child's awareness of anatomical differences.
  • The conflicts associated with this stage are resolved through identification with the same-
  • sex parent. This identification is considered important for the development of the superego.

questions.question: What are self-conscious emotions? How do toddlers express them?
questions.solution_html:
• What are self-conscious emotions? How do toddlers express them?  / [CO3]
  • Self-conscious emotions (embarrassment, pride, envy, shame, guilt) are higher-order
  • evaluations of the self that appear late in the second year (18–24 months), coinciding with
  • the toddler's development of self-awareness. Early signs include eye-lowering
  • (shame/embarrassment) and guilt-like reactions, with pride and envy present by age 3. These
  • emotions require adult instruction for appropriate expression, which is culturally variable.
  • By age 3, these feelings are linked to self-evaluation; for instance, pre-schoolers show greater
  • pride in difficult successes. Crucially, as children mature, school-age children begin to feel
  • pride and guilt without adult monitoring and only experience guilt for intentional
  • wrongdoing, reflecting a more advanced moral sense.

questions.question: Discuss the factors influencing attachment.
questions.solution_html:
• Discuss the factors influencing attachment. / [CO3]
  • Attachment is influenced by several factors related to the caregiver, infant and
  • environment. Caregiver sensitivity and responsiveness are important because infants
  • develop stronger and more secure attachments when caregivers respond appropriately and
  • consistently to their needs. The quality, consistency and emotional availability of
  • caregiving also influence attachment.
  • The infant's temperament can affect the attachment relationship, as some infants are more
  • adaptable or easily soothed than others. Opportunities for interaction and contact, including
  • regular physical and emotional interaction with the caregiver, are also important. In addition,
  • the family environment, emotional climate, parental stress, socioeconomic conditions
  • and other environmental circumstances can influence the quality and security of
  • attachment.

questions.question: Describe the structure of temperament according to Thomas and Chess.
questions.solution_html:
• Describe the structure of temperament according to Thomas and Chess.  /
  • [CO3]
  • Thomas and Chess's model of temperament, consisting of nine dimensions ; 9 Dimensions:
  • Activity Level, Rhythmicity, Distractibility, Approach/Withdrawal, Adaptability, Intensity of
  • Reaction, Threshold of Responsiveness, Quality of Mood, Persistence.
  • Based on the clustering of these dimensions, Thomas and Chess identified three common
  • temperament types:
  • Easy Children (40%): Generally cheerful, quickly establish regular routines, and
  • adapt easily to new experiences.
  • Difficult Children (10%): Irregular in daily routines, slows to accept new
  • experiences, and tend to react negatively and intensely.
  • Slow-to-Warm-Up Children (15%): Inactive, show mild, negative reactions to new
  • stimuli, but slowly adjust over time with repeated exposure.
  • The remaining 35% of children have temperaments that are combinations of these
  • traits.

questions.question: What is phonological awareness, and why is it important?
questions.solution_html:
• What is phonological awareness, and why is it important? / [CO3]
  • Phonological awareness is the ability to recognize and manipulate the sound structure of
  • spoken language. It includes awareness of rhyming words, syllables, words and
  • individual speech sounds or phonemes. Children gradually become able to identify,
  • separate, combine and manipulate these sound units.
  • Phonological awareness is particularly important for literacy development because it helps
  • children understand the relationship between spoken sounds and written symbols. It provides
  • an important foundation for learning to read and spell, as children learn to recognize and
  • manipulate the sounds represented by letters and words.

questions.question: What are the 2 types of morality according to Piaget?
questions.solution_html:
• What are the 2 types of morality according to Piaget?  / [CO3]
  • Heteronomous Morality (5–8 years): Children see rules as fixed, unchangeable laws given
  • by authority figures and must be obeyed. Due to cognitive immaturity and adult control, they
  • show moral realism—believing rules are absolute and not open to change which reinforced
  • by adult figures.
  • Autonomous Morality / Moral Relativism (9-10 and older): With cognitive
  • development, peer interaction, and less adult control, children enter the morality of
  • cooperation stage, viewing rules as flexible and socially agreed upon. They develop a
  • sense of reciprocity, showing equal concern for others’ welfare as for their own.

questions.question: Explain the permissive parenting style with example.
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the permissive parenting style with example. / [CO3]
  • The permissive parenting style is characterized by high warmth and responsiveness but
  • relatively low demandingness and control. Permissive parents are affectionate and
  • accepting but place few rules, demands and limits on their children. They may provide
  • considerable freedom and exercise relatively little discipline or supervision.
  • Such parents may sometimes behave more like a friend than an authority figure. As a
  • result, children may have difficulty developing self-control when clear and consistent
  • boundaries are lacking.
  • Example: A parent may allow a child to decide bedtime, homework and recreational activities
  • without setting consistent rules or consequences, even when the child does not fulfil
  • responsibilities.

questions.question: Explain the advantages and disadvantages of any 2 prenatal diagnostic tests.
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the advantages and disadvantages of any 2 prenatal diagnostic tests.
  • / [CO2]
  • Amniocentesis: It involves removing a small amount of amniotic fluid using a needle and
  • examining fetal cells. It can help identify certain chromosomal abnormalities and genetic
  • disorders, such as Down syndrome and some inherited conditions. Its advantage is that it
  • provides relatively detailed diagnostic information. However, it is an invasive procedure
  • and carries a small risk of complications, including miscarriage.
  • Chorionic Villus Sampling (CVS): It involves obtaining a sample of chorionic villi from
  • the placenta and examining the fetal genetic material. It can identify certain chromosomal
  • and genetic disorders and has the advantage of providing diagnostic information relatively
  • early in pregnancy. Its disadvantage is that it is invasive and carries a small risk of
  • pregnancy-related complications, including miscarriage.

questions.question: How does culture influence cognitive development according to Vygotsky?
questions.solution_html:
• How does culture influence cognitive development according to Vygotsky?
  • / [CO3]
  • Lev Vygotsky's sociocultural theory posits that human cognition is inherently social and
  • language-based, thereby emphasizing the central role of culture on development. Infants
  • are born with basic perceptual, attention, and memory capacities (shared with other
  • animals) that develop through direct contact with the environment during the first two years.
  • However, it is the subsequent rapid growth of language, acquired through cultural and
  • social interaction that leads to a profound change in thinking, transforming these basic
  • capacities into higher-order cognitive processes.

questions.question: According to Piaget how the cognitive ability of a 10 year old child differs from that of a 5 year old child ?
questions.solution_html:
• According to Piaget how the cognitive ability of a 10 year old child differs from that
  • of a 5 year old child ? / [CO3]
  • According to Piaget, a 5-year-old child is generally in the preoperational stage (2–7
  • years). The child can use symbolic thought and language, but logical operations are not yet
  • fully developed. The child may show egocentrism, difficulty taking another person's
  • perspective and difficulty understanding conservation because thinking is strongly
  • influenced by perceptual appearance.
  • A 10-year-old child is generally in the concrete operational stage (7–11 years). The child
  • can perform logical operations on concrete objects and events and develops an
  • understanding of conservation, classification, seriation and reversibility. The child is also
  • better able to consider different aspects of a situation and understand another person's
  • perspective.Thus, the 10-year-old demonstrates more logical, organized and flexible
  • thinking than the 5-year-old.

questions.question: Explain why balanced diets help both growth and learning.
questions.solution_html:
• Explain why balanced diets help both growth and learning. / [CO2]
  • A balanced diet supplies essential nutrients such as proteins, carbohydrates, fats, vitamins
  • and minerals, which are necessary for physical growth, tissue development and normal
  • body functioning. Adequate nutrition is especially important during childhood because the
  • body and brain undergo rapid development.
  • Nutrition also has an important role in brain development and cognitive functioning.
  • Adequate nutrients support attention, memory, concentration and learning. For example,
  • inadequate nutrition can contribute to fatigue, poor concentration and reduced school
  • performance. Nutritional deficiencies may also interfere with normal physical and cognitive
  • development. Thus, a balanced diet supports both healthy physical growth and effective
  • learning.

questions.question: Explain the Conventional Level in Kohlberg’s theory
questions.solution_html:
• Explain Conventional Level in Kohlberg’s theory?
  • At the conventional level, moral reasoning is based on maintaining social rules and order.
  • People obey rules not for self-interest but to preserve relationships and ensure social
  • harmony. The sub stage includes
  • Stage 3 – “Good Boy–Good Girl” Orientation:
  • Moral behaviour aims to gain approval and maintain social harmony through being kind,
  • loyal, respectful, and helpful. Individuals understand ideal reciprocity—the Golden Rule
  • —treats others as you wish to be treated.
  • Stage 4 – Social-Order-Maintaining Orientation:
  • Morality is based on obeying laws and fulfilling duties to maintain social order and
  • cooperation. Moral choices no longer depend on close ties to others. Rules are seen as
  • necessary and must apply equally to everyone.
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Explain in short, the post conventional level in Kohlberg’s theory.
questions.solution_html:
• Explain in short, the post conventional level in Kohlberg's theory. / [CO3]
  • The post-conventional level is the third and highest level in Kohlberg's theory of moral
  • development. At this level, moral reasoning is based on internalized principles and
  • personal moral standards, rather than simply on avoiding punishment, obtaining rewards or
  • gaining social approval.
  • It consists of Stage 5 – Social Contract and Individual Rights, in which individuals
  • recognize that laws are social agreements designed to protect people's rights and welfare and
  • may be changed when they are unjust. Stage 6 – Universal Ethical Principles involves
  • reasoning according to broader principles such as justice, equality and respect for human
  • dignity.

questions.question: How does the expression of happiness change from infancy to toddlerhood?
questions.solution_html:
• How does the expression of happiness change from infancy to toddlerhood?
  • Happiness initially manifests as blissful smiles and later as laughter, contributing to the
  • infant's social, cognitive, and motor development. Newborns smile when full, during REM
  • sleep, or in response to soothing input like gentle touches and the mother's soft voice. The
  • social smile develops between 6 and 10 weeks, followed by laughter around 3-4 months,
  • which signals faster information processing. By the middle of the first year, infants prefer
  • familiar people, and the combined expressions of smiling and laughter strengthen the parent-
  • child bond. By 10-12 months, babies exhibit various types of smiles.

questions.question: Describe the concept of temperament and its significance in child development.
questions.solution_html:
• Describe the concept of temperament and its significance in child development. /
  • [CO3]
  • Temperament refers to relatively stable, biologically influenced individual differences in
  • emotional reactivity, activity level and self-regulation. Children differ in characteristics
  • such as activity level, emotional intensity, adaptability, attention and approach or
  • withdrawal.
  • Temperament influences how children respond to people, situations and changes in their
  • environment. It does not determine development by itself; rather, it interacts with parenting
  • and environmental experiences. Goodness of fit refers to how well the child's temperament
  • matches the expectations and demands of the environment. A good fit between the child's
  • characteristics and the environment can promote better adjustment and positive development.

questions.question: What are the three stages of child birth?

questions.question: What are the survival role of new born reflexes?
questions.solution_html:
• What are the survival role of new born reflexes? / [CO2]
  • Newborn reflexes are automatic and involuntary responses to particular stimuli and serve
  • important survival and adaptive functions during early infancy.
  • The rooting reflex helps the infant turn toward stimulation around the mouth and locate the
  • nipple, while the sucking reflex enables the infant to obtain nourishment. The Moro reflex,
  • which occurs in response to sudden stimulation or a sensation of falling, produces a
  • characteristic protective response. The grasping reflex may also have an early adaptive
  • function. In addition to survival functions, newborn reflexes provide important information
  • about the infant's neurological health and maturation because their presence, strength and
  • disappearance follow characteristic developmental patterns.

questions.question: Explain the substages of Sensory motor stage
questions.solution_html:
• Explain Sub stages of Sensory motor stage
  • Piaget divided the Sensorimotor Stage (birth–2 years) into six sub stages showing how
  • infants move from simple reflexes to mental thinking. In the reflexive stage (0–1 month),
  • behaviour is based on innate reflexes like sucking and grasping. In primary circular
  • reactions (1–4 months), infants repeat actions centered on their own body, such as thumb
  • sucking. During secondary circular reactions (4–8 months), they repeat actions that affect
  • the environment, like shaking a rattle. In the coordination of secondary schemes (8–12
  • months), behaviour becomes intentional and goal-directed; object permanence begins to
  • develop. The tertiary circular reactions (12–18 months) involve active experimentation
  • and curiosity, where infants vary actions to see new results. Finally, in the mental
  • representation stage (18–24 months), children form internal images and symbols, allowing
  • for symbolic play and deferred imitation and immediate problem solving
